[M] Each mission post will be more detailed than this, but this should work well as a basic overview.

With the recent advancement of a lightweight, solar powered, remote controlled excavator as well as an efficient electrolysis machine capable of converting soil into water and air (each built on previously existing technology), the Australian, US and UK space agencies have announced their intentions to collaborate to create a sub-surface base on the rim of the moon’s Peary crater.

The project's first mission will be to send a slightly modified version of the ‘Luto’ excavator to the bases’ proposed location on the rim of the Peary crater at the moon’s north pole. Once on the surface, the excavator will begin to autonomously dig a 100x100 meter cavern that will be used as a starting point for the base. If at any time the excavator is unable to perform its functions autonomously, it will be possible for humans to remotely intervene from earth.

Once the cavern has been completed, the excavator will coat it’s walls with a layer of spray-on insulating foam to allow us to keep the base at a steady temperature.

Our second mission will be to send an array of solar panels to the base to serve as its power source. With the location of the base being at the Moon’s north pole, these solar panels will be in constant view of the sun and will continuously gather energy day or night.

The Ariane 5 ES can carry 763 Kyocera KD315GX-LPB solar panels at once (though we'll round this down to 760) and each panel has a maximum power of roughly 315 watts (rounding down to 300), and we'll be using them 24/7, so each will produce roughly 7200KWh a year, meaning that all 760 of them together will generate roughly 5,470,000KWh of electricity.

The average American household requires 10,932KWh a year to operate (rounding down to 10,900KWh) and the average number of people in a US household (going off 2014 figures) is about 3.13 (rounding down to 3) meaning each individual uses about 3600KWh a year in a year.

Not taking into account the power drawn by life support systems, the base would produce enough energy to comfortably house roughly 1500 individuals. Our first manned mission however, will only send 20 individuals to the base as there will not yet be sufficient room for large amounts of people.

Our third mission will send a yet-to-be developed rover based on NASA’s ‘Curiosity’ to the base. The rover will be capable of performing precision tasks such as connecting the solar panel array and electrolysis machine to the structure, which it will achieve via a series of mechanical arms that will replace the various scientific tools on board the original Curiosity design.

Our fourth mission will be to send up various essentials to the base such as: an airlock, regular and UV and light bulbs, assorted seeds, flat packed furniture and inflatable rooms that will serve to section off areas of the base until more permanent structures can be developed. Once the payload has been delivered, our rover will begin begin preparing the base for human habitation and, once possible, will set up an indoor farm to serve as a source of food for it’s inhabitants.

Our final mission of the initial project will be sending 20 individuals to the base who will improve on the work of the rover and extend the size of the base to allow for additional inhabitants.

As the project has the potential to go wrong in a variety of different ways ASA, NASA and UKSA are not yet able to provide an estimated date for its completion.
